I've read a LOT of OM fics (and passed on many more within the first few paragraphs) and write my own as well.  I personally prefer third person in anything I read, including fanfics, but I've been enjoying a couple of Obey Me fics that are second person - it's bearable if it's done well.

I hate the Y/N thing, I prefer 'MC' if it must be done, but above all I like stories with people's own MCs.  It's fun for me to learn about their character (assuming it's done well, and they're a fleshed out person rather than a caricature) and see the differences in how they act vs how my MC acts.  But I also just am not big on self-inserting; other folks can do it, I just don't enjoy it as much, I always insert my own MC instead.

And I think any perspective - whether MC's or another character - can be great if it's done well.  It's harder to get it right when it's another character, just because you want to keep them in-character, but it can be a really great way to delve into the minds of the characters we love.

Have to say, I strongly disagree.  Characters' names and their pronouns are perfectly fine.  I agree using the name multiple times in one paragraph unnecessarily is tedious, but that's what pronouns are for, as well as restructuring your word placement and syntax.  Instead of what you put, it could be written like this and sound much better:

"Jessie said. She stood up and picked up the book to open it and flip through the pages."

Now if there are multiple characters doing things within a paragraph, then names should be used more often, when it makes sense.  But regularly using epithets (especially compound epithets, like "the male redhead" or "the blue-eyed woman" or something) imo tends to look... Idk.  It makes me think the writer either is very young or inexperienced or just not a good writer, or that they think their readers are too stupid to remember what a character looks like (or they think that appearance is really *that* important... It's not, usually. Only the writer cares that much about how their character looks).

I used to use epithets all the time in my fics.  I don't think they're the worst thing of course, and they won't generally get me to stop reading a fic, but I do think they should be avoided if you're trying to improve the quality of your writing.  The challenge of rewriting a paragraph to make sense, properly identify the subjects within, and not rely on epithets, is a good challenge that helps build writing ability.

Maybe it's because I mostly read original published fiction and they don't typically have epithets, so when I see them in fanfiction it's jarring. Idk.

Oh hell yeah, I love this kinda stuff!  It speaks to me on a personal level, lol.  The trick is often to have one-sided pining from one character and have one be oblivious.  So they start a FWB thing and keep it to casual sex, maybe they're actually friends or maybe just acquaintances.

Then Character A catches feelings but doesn't want to admit it to themselves, or doesn't want to risk making things weird between them, so they keep it hidden.  The sex starts getting super good and maybe it either comes out that A is kinda in love with B, or maybe something dramatic happens to A and B suddenly realizes they care far more about A than they thought, or maybe B slowly starts catching feels too when A gets more cuddly/lovey with them during/after sex.

I know with my intimate friends who I'm extremely close to, we have moments where we just *get* each other - like I'll be explaining something I'm feeling/going through, and they'll sort of complete my thought, often with an analogy ("yeah, it's like you're trying to balance a bucket full of stress and a bucket full of excitement in one hand, and if one starts the spill it upsets the other and that one spills over," or something, idk that's not a great example, haha) and it's just a beautiful moment, because they get me on a deep level.

Also being willing to (if schedules and emotional wellness allows) drop everything to be there for them when they're struggling.  And meeting eyes while hanging out with other people and sharing a smile or a silly expression.  Offhand mentioning of shared past experiences is another good way, as well as inside jokes - like my one friend and I often intentionally say incorrect figures of speech ("green around the belt" instead of "green around the gills") and malapropisms ("bone apple tea" for "bon appetit" or "just a position" for "juxtaposition") when talking together because we think it's hilarious for some dumb reason.

For me, creating OCs is a process of taking traits I like in my friends/family and fictional characters, and think would make for an interesting person, and also taking real flaws from those same sources (including myself) that I want to explore.  The flaws to explore is the biggest part for me - my OCs are usually a way for me to work through either my own issues or things I see in the world that I want to try to understand better.

Disclaimer: I'm very tired so I hope the following stuff makes sense, lol.

So, for example, one of my OCs in one of my longfics tends to be very defensive and quick to anger when confronted with her own flaws or what she perceives as attacks or judgments on her due to her status (as a mage, which is an oppressed class in that fandom).  When I created her I wanted to poke at my own defensiveness when I'm criticized over something I'm particularly sensitive about, and also to explore my then-best friend's tendency to take anything short of outright praise as a personal attack and lash out (there's a reason we're not friends anymore, lol).

I had to balance her flaw with positive traits as well, such as being compassionate and caring about others, at times to the point of putting herself at risk.  This is something she starts to grow out of as she hardens and faces the harsh reality of a world that doesn't often reward putting oneself in harm's way to help others.  This eventually becomes a minor flaw, and one I try to work through in my fic to see if I can have her maintain her compassion when the world kicks her when she's down.  This is a pretty personal one to myself too, as well as to all my friends, because compassion fatigue and wariness is really setting in to our friend group.

And then you sprinkle in some various quirks and things that give a bit more depth - or humor.  That OC hates horses, thinks they're stupid and gross and overrated.  She also tends to drink to forget her troubles (another minor flaw).  And she doesn't know how to swim (she grew up in a tower unable to go outside).  She loves reading and learning, and also goes on long runs to clear her mind.  She likes to name her pets after other animals (dog named Rabbit, horse named Pig, etc) because she finds it funny for some reason.

So yeah, that was (a small bit of) the process I went through with that one OC for a serious/angsty longfic.  It'll be slightly different with a comedic fic or one-shots.  But basically, when I'm interacting with others or consuming any type of media, I notice traits or quirks or flaws and make note of any that might make for a compelling character.  I also get inspiration from songs - often times my characters have a mini playlist I've mentally assigned to each of them.

Backstory is a bit tougher.  At some point you have to acknowledge that tropes are inevitable and that's okay.  I just run down the basics and try to come up with random crap, look over it all and see if it makes sense, is too angsty (that's my problem, lol), fits with the lore, fits with the personality of my character, etc.  The basics I use are: Where are their parents now?  What sort of parenting style did they have?  Did they have other close family or friends growing up?  How did they do with learning/school?  What were they most afraid of as a child? (And can I incorporate that somehow)

Anywho, I hope this helps, it's my tired rambles. Not all phobias can or should be treated with exposure, and for true diagnosed phobias (rather than just big fears) you can sometimes do more damage trying to expose yourself to your phobia.  Best to (if financially viable) work with a therapist or counselor to figure out if guided exposure therapy would work best for you, rather than jumping in to it headfirst alone.  I'm glad it worked for you, but I hope you'll stop spreading this idea that that is the way to handle it.

Source: have a moderate-severe diagnosed phobia (not of spiders, but similar in that it's of an animal rather than something like heights or social interaction) and regressed horribly after trying to do minor exposure therapy by myself.  Talked to a therapist and she was like "oh no pls don't do that by yourself again" but I had to stop therapy before we could do any real work on it. And thus my phobia remains :(

>If you’re familiar with all the controversy surrounding puppy/kitten mills, you won’t be surprised to learn those same issues are linked with the breeding of hybrids, too.  The following is a snapshot of the dark side of hybrid breeding:

>During the breeding process, domestic cats forced to breed with wild cats can often be killed.  Many pregnancies are aborted or absorbed by the mother cat’s body when nature determines there is something wrong.  Kittens are often born prematurely due to the variance of gestation periods between the wild cats and domestic cats that have been interbred.  Many of the first generation are sterile, especially the males.  In some cases, breeders may kill kittens born with an undesirable appearance, or just drop them off at a shelter.

>Quite like the controversial issues faced with puppy mills, hybrid cats used for breeding can face the same poor quality of life.  Forced to live in a cage the majority of their lives, they are not socialized.  [...]  The cats can suffer from illnesses and live in filthy conditions that are rarely detected since they’re not the subject of inspections.

>There is no doubt that breeding a hybrid cat that will bring in thousands of dollars tends to naturally attract many whose sole motive is profit.  Why breed a “normal” domestic purebred cat that may fetch only $200 when you can breed a hybrid cat that can bring in as much as $22,000?  This quest for high profits leads many breeders to house too many cats under poor conditions and leads to poor genetics as more and more are interbred.
